title: Abu Musa al-Ash'ari
hookLine: a companion whose recitation the Prophet ﷺ likened to the pipes of the family of Dawud

cards: Night in Medina. A man is reciting the Qur'an, for no one in particular. He doesn't know that out in the dark, someone has stopped to listen.

The next day the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, tells him: if only you had seen me last night, listening to your recitation. Then a compliment: you have been given one of the pipes of the family of Dawud.
Today: Abu Musa al-Ash'ari, a man from Yemen with a voice worth stopping for.

teach.b: The word in the hadith is mizmar, a reed pipe, a wind instrument. Dawud, the prophet David, is remembered in the Qur'an as one with whom the mountains and the birds joined in praise.
So the Prophet was saying: your voice carries something of that. Muslim and Bukhari both record it. But here's the turn.
Abu Musa also narrates a very different lesson about voices. On a journey, he reports, the companions were climbing and calling out God is greatest at the top of their lungs.
And the Prophet told them to go easy on themselves.
You are not calling on someone deaf or absent, he said. You are calling on One who hears, and who is near. Put the two reports side by side.
The sweet voice was heard at night, unplanned, not on a stage. The loud voices were gently quieted.
Beauty in recitation, in these reports, is not about volume. It's about a sense that the One addressed is close. A third picture of Abu Musa's people fits.

Bukhari records the Prophet praising the Ash'aris, Abu Musa's tribe, because when their food ran low they gathered everything they had on one cloth and shared it out equally. They are from me, he said, and I am from them.
A people known for sharing, and one of them known for a voice. Neither the food nor the voice was kept to themselves.

how: Muslims value beautiful, careful recitation of the Qur'an (tajwid), and Abu Musa's reported gift comes up when people speak of reciting with a lovely voice.

games.q: you're on a journey with the Prophet. at every rise the group is shouting God is greatest at full volume. what does the Prophet say?
o: louder, so the whole valley hears.
go easy: you call on One who hears and is near.
stop praising God on the road.
games.why: Abu Musa reports he told them to go easy on themselves: you are not calling on one deaf or absent, but One who hears, and is near.

practice: If you know a short surah, or al-Fatiha, say it now almost under your breath, slowly, giving each letter its place and not rushing the long vowels.
If you don't recite, do the same with any words that matter to you, or simply listen to your breathing as if it were a sound worth tending. Not loud. Close, as if speaking to someone who is near.

wordCard.voice: Abu Musa. A companion from Yemen whose recitation the Prophet compared to a pipe of the family of Dawud, and who also reported: you call on One who hears, and is near. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: a reed pipe, the word in the hadith about Abu Musa's voice.

carryVoice: Your line: a voice like Dawud's. Beauty is closeness, not volume. Day eight hundred fifty-nine, done.
